questions.question: A probability can never be...
questions.explanation: Probabilities run from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain). A result above 1 or below 0 signals a mistake in your counting.

questions.question: A fair die is rolled once. What is P(even number)?
questions.explanation: The even outcomes are {2, 4, 6}: 3 of 6 equally likely outcomes, so 3/6 = 1/2.

questions.question: Two fair coins are flipped. What is P(exactly one head)?
questions.explanation: List the sequences HH, HT, TH, TT. Exactly one head occurs in HT and TH, so 2/4 = 1/2. Listing 'zero, one, two heads' would give the wrong 1/3, because those are not equally likely.

questions.question: Two fair dice are rolled. What is P(sum = 7)?
questions.explanation: There are 36 equally likely pairs, and 6 of them sum to 7 (1+6, 2+5, 3+4, 4+3, 5+2, 6+1). 6/36 = 1/6.

questions.question: A fair coin is flipped 3 times. What is P(at least one head)?
questions.explanation: Use the complement. The only way to get no heads is TTT, probability 1/8. So P(at least one head) = 1 − 1/8 = 7/8.

questions.question: After 10 coin flips you have 7 heads. What does the Law of Large Numbers say?
options: The experimental proportion tends toward 0.5 as flips accumulate, but it makes no promise about the next flip
The next flips must even it out
questions.explanation: Over many trials the experimental proportion settles near the true probability. The coin has no memory, so there is no 'catching up'. Early imbalance simply gets diluted by later flips.
